story: The Sanriku coast was shaped by hundreds of millions of years of movement in the Earth's crust. In the north the land has been lifted, and the sea has cut it into sheer cliffs: at Kitayamazaki and Unosu they stand around two hundred metres high, and the coast is called the Alps of the sea. Further south the land has sunk, the sea has flooded the valleys, and the shore becomes a ria coast of long inlets and headlands — the Hakozaki Peninsula, the Goishi coast, Shizugawa Bay and the Oshika Peninsula. Along the way are limestone blowholes, granite pavements and the sharp white rocks of Jodogahama.

In summer a cold sea fog called yamase rolls in off the Pacific and keeps the coast cool, so plants that normally grow high in the mountains flower at sea level. White-flowered rhododendrons cling to the cliffs of Kitayamazaki, and on the Tanesashi coast beach plants and mountain flowers bloom side by side. The cliffs and islands hold seabird colonies — tens of thousands of black-tailed gulls arrive on Kabushima at Hachinohe from early March — and eelgrass beds in the shallow bays shelter fish and wintering brant geese.

This is one of Japan's great fishing coasts, with the ports of Hachinohe, Miyako, Kamaishi, Ōfunato, Kesennuma and Ishinomaki, oyster rafts in the bays, and the northernmost community of ama, women who dive for sea urchin and abalone, at Kosode. It is also a coast that has been struck again and again by tsunamis. The 1896 tsunami snapped the top off Oreishi, a sixteen-metre rock pillar at Karakuwa. On 11 March 2011 the Great East Japan Earthquake sent a tsunami along the whole of this shore; at Rikuzentakata it swept away a forest of some 70,000 pines and left a single tree standing.

Most of this coast, from Kuji to Kesennuma, had been protected since 1955 as Rikuchu Kaigan National Park. After 2011 the Ministry of the Environment rebuilt it as a park meant to serve the recovery: in May 2013 it was extended north to Tanesashi and renamed Sanriku Fukko — 'Sanriku reconstruction' — and in 2015 it took in the Minami-Sanriku Kinkazan Quasi-National Park and reached south to the Oshika Peninsula. The Michinoku Coastal Trail now links the coast for about a thousand kilometres, and many visitors come specifically to learn about disaster and recovery.
howItWorks: The park is a narrow strip of headlands, beaches and offshore islands running through eighteen municipalities in Aomori, Iwate and Miyagi. Of its 28,539 hectares on land, Aomori holds 2,423, Iwate 11,232 and Miyagi 14,884. The big fishing ports — Hachinohe, Miyako, Kamaishi, Ōfunato, Kesennuma and Ishinomaki — lie along it. In Miyagi the Ministry cannot yet give a breakdown of who owns the land, because buy-ups for reconstruction after the tsunami have changed so much of it.

Only 848 hectares are special protection zone, where picking any plant, collecting fallen leaves or branches, catching animals or lighting a fire needs a permit from the Minister of the Environment. Some 25,460 hectares are special zone, where building, felling, quarrying and picking listed plants need a permit, and 2,229 are ordinary zone. Offshore, marine park zones protect the sea floor and its life off Kesennuma, in Yamada Bay and along the coast of Minamisanriku, where taking listed animals and seaweeds is controlled.

Shizugawa Bay at Minamisanriku, with its seaweed and eelgrass beds, has been a Ramsar wetland since 2018. Most of the Sanriku coast, from Hachinohe to Kesennuma, is also a geopark — the largest in Japan — and its geosites overlap the park. At Jodogahama, Miyako city closes the coast road to private cars at night all year and all day from April to October, and runs a free loop bus on weekends and holidays in season.

sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-tanesashi-coast: Natural lawn running right down to the sea, shaped by horse grazing since long ago, with a coastal path past flowers that mix beach and mountain species.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-kabushima: A small hill at Hachinohe crowned by a shrine to Benzaiten, where tens of thousands of black-tailed gulls nest from March. The trail's northern start.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-kitayamazaki: Two-hundred-metre cliffs, headlands and sea caves, the most famous view on the coast. Clifftop paths, and tours in small fishing boats called sappa.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-jodogahama: A cove of sharp white rocks, pines and deep blue water near Miyako, with a summer swimming beach and boats into the sea caves.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-goishi-coast-and-an: Sawtooth cliffs near Ōfunato and a sea rock pierced by three large holes, which small boats can pass through.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-miracle-pine: At Rikuzentakata, the one pine left standing when the 2011 tsunami swept away the Takata Matsubara forest, preserved as a monument after it died.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-ogama-hanzo: Limestone coast on the Karakuwa Peninsula with Oreishi, a sixteen-metre pillar whose top was broken off by the 1896 tsunami.
sightNotes.poi-jp-sanriku-fukko-kinkasan: A sacred, wooded island off the Oshika Peninsula, where deer, held to be messengers of the gods, roam freely.

entrances: Hachinohe and the Tanesashi coast, at the northern end
Ōfunato and Rikuzentakata, for the Goishi coast and the Miracle Pine
Kesennuma and Minamisanriku, for Karakuwa and Shizugawa Bay
Ishinomaki, for the Oshika Peninsula and Kinkasan
planYourVisit.reservations: No reservation is needed to enter the park. Boat tours, sappa-boat rides and ama diving demonstrations run in season and are booked locally; check before you go with each town.
permits: No permit is needed to walk the Michinoku Coastal Trail; taking listed sea life in the marine park zones is controlled
camping: Campsites along the Michinoku Coastal Trail; ask at the trail centres and visitor centres
lodging: The port cities — Hachinohe, Miyako, Kamaishi, Ōfunato, Kesennuma and Ishinomaki
seasonalClosures: The Jodogahama coast road is closed to private cars all day from April to October and every night all year

chronology.text: The Meiji Sanriku tsunami snaps the top off Oreishi at Karakuwa.
Rikuchu Kaigan National Park is designated on 2 May.
The park is extended south to Iwaisaki in Kesennuma.
The park is extended north, and marine park zones are designated off Kesennuma.
On 11 March the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami devastate the coast.
On 24 May the park is extended north to the Tanesashi coast and renamed Sanriku Fukko National Park.
Minami-Sanriku Kinkazan Quasi-National Park is incorporated, extending the park south to the Oshika Peninsula.
Shizugawa Bay is added, becomes a Ramsar wetland, and new marine park zones are designated in Yamada Bay and off Minamisanriku.

safety: This coast is struck by tsunamis. If you feel a strong or long earthquake, or hear a warning, move to high ground at once without waiting to see the sea, and follow the evacuation signs posted along the coast and the trail.
The cliffs at Kitayamazaki and Unosu are two hundred metres high. Keep to the paths and lookouts, and keep off wave-washed rocks.
Asiatic black bears (tsukinowaguma) live in the hills of northern Honshu. On forest sections of the trail, make noise and check local warnings.
Sea fog can close in quickly in summer; carry a map and keep to the path.
regulations: Do not collect shellfish, sea urchin or seaweed: they are fished commercially here, and taking listed species in the marine park zones needs a permit.
Picking any plant, collecting fallen branches, catching animals or lighting a fire in the special protection zone needs a permit.
Respect the memorials and the reconstruction sites; many places on this coast are also places of loss.

weather: Summers are cool, often grey with the yamase sea fog, which is why alpine flowers grow on the cliffs. Spring brings the gulls back to Kabushima from early March and azaleas to the hilltops — Tatsuganeyama in mid-May, Hashikami-dake in early June — and early summer the coastal flowers at Tanesashi. Summer is the season for swimming at Jodogahama and for watching the ama dive at Kosode. Brant geese winter in Shizugawa Bay.
directions: The Tohoku Shinkansen runs along the inland side of the park; pick the station nearest your section. From Hachinohe, the JR Hachinohe Line reaches Tanesashi-Kaigan Station in about 33 minutes. From Morioka, the JR Yamada Line or a bus reaches Miyako in about two hours, and the Sanriku Railway's Rias Line runs along much of the Iwate coast between Sakari (Ōfunato) and Kuji. From Ichinoseki, the JR Ōfunato Line reaches Kesennuma, and JR's bus rapid transit (BRT) serves most of the coast south of Ōfunato. A car gives the most freedom along the coast.
